passage.title: The Mold That Changed Medicine
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
Before 1940, a tiny scratch from a rose thorn or a scraped knee could turn into a deadly illness. Doctors had no drug that could kill bad germs in the blood without hurting good cells too. In the fall of 1928, a Scottish doctor named Alexander Fleming came back to his London lab after a trip. Before leaving, he had stacked several glass dishes of bacteria on a corner bench. As he checked the pile, one open dish caught his eye. A stray speck of mold had drifted in through the air and contaminated the gel.

Most lab workers would have tossed the spoiled glass dish straight into the wash bin. Fleming, though, stopped to look closely at the strange pattern on the plate. Around the pale green patch of mold, the thick colonies of harmful germs had been completely dissolved by a clear ring of liquid. Something oozing from the green bread mold was stopping the bad germs from growing. Fleming named this active mold juice penicillin.

Fleming knew the mold juice was potent against germs, yet he could not turn it into a lasting drug on his own. The raw liquid was extremely fragile and lost its germ-fighting power within days. For ten years, Fleming tried to pull the pure healing stuff out of the thin broth. Each time, he failed. At last, he printed his notes in a book and hoped that skilled chemists might solve the puzzle.

In 1938, a team at Oxford led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain read Fleming's notes and took up the task. Working day and night with giant milk churns, bath trays, and clay bedpans, they grew gallons of the green mold. Chain found a way to freeze-dry the broth so the delicate medicine could be extracted as a stable brown powder without losing its strength. When they gave the powder to sick mice in 1940, the mice got well fast.

By 1943, big plants in the United States were using deep vats and corn water to brew the drug. Soon they made enough of the powder to save thousands of hurt troops. What began as an accidental speck of mold on a messy lab bench became a life-saving drug only after a second team figured out how to purify and store it.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"Around the pale green patch of mold, the thick colonies of harmful germs had been completely dissolved by a clear ring of liquid."

In this sentence, what actually dissolved the colonies of harmful germs?

options.text: The thick colonies of harmful germs
options.childFeedback: The thick colonies of harmful germs received the action—they were dissolved by the clear ring of liquid, instead of dissolving themselves!

options.text: A sharp rose thorn placed on the glass plate
options.childFeedback: A rose thorn is only mentioned in Paragraph 1 as an example of a cut that could cause an infection; there was no thorn on Fleming's glass dish.

options.text: Hot soap and water from the laboratory wash bin
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 says Fleming stopped instead of tossing the dish into the wash bin, so soap and water didn't dissolve the germs—the mold's clear liquid did.

options.text: A clear ring of liquid oozing from the mold
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, the passive verb 'had been completely dissolved by' tells us that 'a clear ring of liquid' oozing from the green mold is what wiped out the harmful germs.

questions.provingSentenceText: Around the pale green patch of mold, the thick colonies of harmful germs had been completely dissolved by a clear ring of liquid.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, the passive verb 'had been completely dissolved by' tells us that 'a clear ring of liquid' oozing from the green mold is what wiped out the harmful germs.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive-voice sentence, 'the thick colonies of harmful germs' is the receiver of the action. The true actor performing 'had been dissolved' comes after 'by': 'a clear ring of liquid' (Option B).
questions.retryHint: Look right after 'had been completely dissolved by' in Paragraph 2 to see what actually dissolved the germ colonies.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 4:

"Chain found a way to freeze-dry the broth so the delicate medicine could be extracted as a stable brown powder without losing its strength."

What does the word "extracted" mean as it is used in this sentence?

options.text: Hidden inside a locked medical journal for ten years
options.childFeedback: Fleming printed his notes in a book in Paragraph 3 so chemists COULD read them, not to hide them! 'Extracted' means pulled out from the liquid broth.

options.text: Thrown away into a laboratory trash can
options.childFeedback: Throwing the medicine in a trash can is the opposite of saving it! Chain freeze-dried the broth so the pure powder could be pulled out and kept.

options.text: Pulled out and separated from a liquid mixture
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, 'extracted' means pulled out and separated from a liquid mixture. Chain freeze-dried the watery mold broth to pull out the pure medicine as a stable brown powder.

options.text: Mixed with harmful germs to make the bacteria grow faster
options.childFeedback: Penicillin kills harmful germs rather than making them grow faster! 'Extracted' describes separating the pure medicine powder from the liquid broth.

questions.provingSentenceText: Chain found a way to freeze-dry the broth so the delicate medicine could be extracted as a stable brown powder without losing its strength.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 4, 'extracted' means pulled out and separated from a liquid mixture. Chain freeze-dried the watery mold broth to pull out the pure medicine as a stable brown powder.
questions.parentExplanation: The Latin root 'ex- + trahere' means to draw out. In context, Chain freeze-dried the liquid broth so the pure medicine could be drawn out and separated as a stable brown powder (Option A).
questions.retryHint: Connect 'extracted' in Paragraph 4 to what Fleming tried to do in Paragraph 3: 'pull the pure healing stuff out of the thin broth.'

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 3, why was Alexander Fleming unable to treat patients with penicillin right after he discovered it in 1928?

options.text: He accidentally threw the glass dish into the wash bin before naming the mold.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 specifically says that while most lab workers would have tossed the dish into the wash bin, Fleming stopped to study it and saved the mold.

options.text: The raw mold liquid was unstable and lost its germ-fighting power within a few days.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 explains that raw penicillin liquid was extremely fragile and lost its germ-fighting power within days, and for ten years Fleming could not pull out the pure medicine on his own.

options.text: Hospitals in London refused to use any medicine discovered during a summer trip.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 never says London hospitals refused the medicine because of a summer trip; the problem was that the raw liquid spoiled within days.

options.text: The green mold only dissolved healthy human cells and left harmful germs alone.
options.childFeedback: Paragraphs 1 and 2 show the exact opposite: penicillin dissolved harmful germs without hurting good human cells.

questions.provingSentenceText: The raw liquid was extremely fragile and lost its germ-fighting power within days.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 3 explains that raw penicillin liquid was extremely fragile and lost its germ-fighting power within days, and for ten years Fleming could not pull out the pure medicine on his own.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 3 explains that although Fleming knew the mold juice was potent, 'The raw liquid was extremely fragile and lost its germ-fighting power within days,' preventing him from turning it into a usable drug on his own (Option A).
questions.retryHint: Check the second sentence of Paragraph 3 to see what happened to the raw mold liquid within a few days.

questions.prompt: Which evidence does the author provide in Paragraph 4 to support the claim that turning penicillin into a usable drug required clever chemistry?

options.text: Ernst Chain freeze-dried the mold broth to extract a stable brown powder that cured sick mice.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 4 proves that clever chemistry was needed by showing how Ernst Chain freeze-dried the fragile mold broth to extract a stable brown powder that kept its strength and cured sick mice.

options.text: Fleming left several glass dishes of bacteria stacked on a corner bench in London.
options.childFeedback: Stacking dishes on a bench in Paragraph 1 explains how the accidental mold landed in 1928, not the chemistry used ten years later in Paragraph 4.

options.text: A tiny scratch from a rose thorn could cause a dangerous illness before 1940.
options.childFeedback: The rose thorn example in Paragraph 1 only shows why doctors needed a germ-fighting drug before 1940, not how chemists purified penicillin.

options.text: Most researchers tossed spoiled glass dishes straight into the laboratory wash bin.
options.childFeedback: Tossing spoiled dishes into the wash bin in Paragraph 2 only contrasts other lab workers with Fleming, not how Chain purified the drug.

questions.provingSentenceText: Chain found a way to freeze-dry the broth so the delicate medicine could be extracted as a stable brown powder without losing its strength.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 4 proves that clever chemistry was needed by showing how Ernst Chain freeze-dried the fragile mold broth to extract a stable brown powder that kept its strength and cured sick mice.
questions.parentExplanation: Aligned to ELAGSE5RI8, the author proves the importance of chemical purification by showing how Ernst Chain freeze-dried the broth into a stable brown powder that kept its strength and cured sick mice (Option B).
questions.retryHint: Look in Paragraph 4 for the specific chemical breakthrough that solved the problem of the fragile liquid losing its power.

questions.prompt: PART A: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?

options.text: Scientists should always leave their laboratory windows open during summer vacation so mold can grow.
options.childFeedback: The author isn't telling scientists to leave lab windows open! The stray mold spore was a lucky accident that still required years of hard chemistry to become medicine.

options.text: Penicillin became a life-saving medicine because Fleming noticed an accidental mold spore and later scientists found a way to purify it.
options.childFeedback: The passage traces how two steps were needed to change medicine: first Fleming noticed the accidental mold killing germs in 1928, and later Florey and Chain's team figured out how to purify and store it.

options.text: Milk churns and clay bedpans are better for growing bacteria than glass dishes.
options.childFeedback: Milk churns and bedpans in Paragraph 4 were just the makeshift containers the Oxford team used to grow mold, not the main idea of the article.

options.text: Howard Florey and Ernst Chain proved that Alexander Fleming's 1928 notes were completely wrong.
options.childFeedback: Florey and Chain didn't prove Fleming's notes wrong—Paragraph 4 says they built on his notes and solved the purification puzzle he had hoped chemists would tackle!

questions.provingSentenceText: What began as an accidental speck of mold on a messy lab bench became a life-saving drug only after a second team figured out how to purify and store it.
questions.childTip: The passage traces how two steps were needed to change medicine: first Fleming noticed the accidental mold killing germs in 1928, and later Florey and Chain's team figured out how to purify and store it.
questions.parentExplanation: The passage traces how two stages of scientific work—Fleming's sharp observation in 1928 and Florey and Chain's purification ten years later—combined to create usable penicillin (Option A).
questions.retryHint: Read the last sentence of Paragraph 5 to see how both Fleming's 1928 discovery and the second team's purification work were needed.

questions.prompt: PART B: Which quotation from the passage best supports the correct answer to Question 5?

options.text: "Before 1940, a tiny scratch from a rose thorn or a scraped knee could turn into a deadly illness."
options.childFeedback: This opening line from Paragraph 1 only explains how dangerous small cuts were before 1940, without mentioning Fleming's mold or how it was purified.

options.text: "Before leaving, he had stacked several glass dishes of bacteria on a corner bench."
options.childFeedback: This detail from Paragraph 1 only sets the scene in Fleming's lab before he even noticed the mold or anyone purified it.

options.text: "Working day and night with giant milk churns, bath trays, and clay bedpans, they grew gallons of the green mold."
options.childFeedback: This sentence from Paragraph 4 only describes the containers used to grow extra mold, leaving out Fleming's discovery and the purification breakthrough.

options.text: "What began as an accidental speck of mold on a messy lab bench became a life-saving drug only after a second team figured out how to purify and store it."
options.childFeedback: This final sentence from Paragraph 5 directly supports Question 5 by connecting Fleming's accidental mold discovery on a lab bench to the second team's work purifying and storing the drug.

questions.provingSentenceText: What began as an accidental speck of mold on a messy lab bench became a life-saving drug only after a second team figured out how to purify and store it.
questions.childTip: This final sentence from Paragraph 5 directly supports Question 5 by connecting Fleming's accidental mold discovery on a lab bench to the second team's work purifying and storing the drug.
questions.parentExplanation: Option D directly proves the central idea in Part A by summarizing how both Fleming's observation and the Oxford team's purification were essential to creating penicillin.
questions.retryHint: Check the closing sentence of Paragraph 5 connecting the accidental speck of mold on a lab bench to the second team.
